items.q: What is Yellowstone's record low temperature?
items.f: It was recorded in 1933 near the West Entrance. The park's record high is 99°F, set at Mammoth in 2002.

items.q: What is the highest point in Yellowstone National Park?
items.f: Eagle Peak reaches 11,358 feet. The park's lowest point is Reese Creek, at 5,282 feet.

items.q: About how many earthquakes does Yellowstone have each year?
items.f: Yellowstone sits on an active volcano and has one of the world's largest calderas, about 45 by 30 miles.

items.q: Which Yellowstone hotel, designed by Robert Reamer and built in 1903–04, is one of the few log hotels left in the U.S.?
items.f: The inn is a National Historic Landmark. Its lobby ceiling is 65 feet high.

items.q: About how much of Yellowstone burned in the fires of 1988?
items.f: In total, 793,880 acres of the park burned that summer.

items.q: Which Yellowstone hydrothermal features can reach temperatures as high as 280°F?
items.f: The NPS says steam vents are often superheated, reaching temperatures as high as 280°F.

items.q: About how many mammal species live in Yellowstone?
items.f: They include two kinds of bears and seven native hoofed mammals.

items.q: Yellowstone Lake is North America's largest freshwater lake above what elevation?
items.f: The lake sits at 7,733 feet. It has 141 miles of shoreline and is up to 430 feet deep.

items.q: Which 1870 expedition gave Old Faithful its name?
items.f: The explorers named the geyser for how regularly it erupted.
items.s: National Park Service: Old Faithful Geyser

items.q: Isa Lake, on the Continental Divide at Craig Pass, was once probably the only lake on Earth to drain naturally into what?
items.f: The NPS says this may now happen only at peak snowmelt after winters with deep snow.

items.q: Which animal became the official U.S. national mammal in 2016?
items.f: President Obama signed the National Bison Legacy Act on May 9, 2016.
items.s: National Park Service: America's New National Mammal

items.q: The NPS calls Yellowstone's Lamar Buffalo Ranch the birthplace of what?
items.f: It was the first effort to save a wild species through intensive management.
items.s: National Park Service: Lamar Buffalo Ranch

items.q: Which Yellowstone geyser shoots at an angle across the Firehole River?
items.f: Riverside is in the Upper Geyser Basin, not far from Old Faithful.

items.q: How tall is the Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River?
items.f: Yellowstone has about 290 waterfalls, and the Lower Falls is the tallest one near a road.

items.q: Which group took charge of Yellowstone in 1886?
items.f: The Army arrived on August 20, 1886, and later built Fort Yellowstone at Mammoth. Many of its red-roofed buildings are still in use.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: Yellowstone stretches into three states. Which of these is NOT one of them?
items.f: About 96% of the park is in Wyoming, 3% in Montana and 1% in Idaho.

items.q: Which pass is the trailhead for the popular hike up Mount Washburn?
items.f: The trailhead parking lot is 4.5 miles north of Canyon Junction.
items.s: National Park Service: Dunraven Pass–Mount Washburn Trail

items.q: Which animal is the most numerous large mammal in Yellowstone?
items.f: In summer, 10,000 to 20,000 elk live in the park. Fewer than 2,000 stay through the winter.

items.q: Yellowstone's colorful bubbling mudpots are sometimes called what?
items.f: Minerals in the mud give mudpots so many colors that they earned the nickname 'paint pots.'

items.q: A microbe discovered in a Yellowstone hot spring made which scientific tool possible?
items.f: Thomas Brock and Hudson Freeze described Thermus aquaticus in 1969. Its heat-resistant enzyme, Taq polymerase, makes PCR work.
items.s: National Park Service: Discovering Life in Yellowstone

items.q: In what year was Yellowstone established as the world's first national park?
items.f: President Ulysses S. Grant signed the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act on March 1, 1872.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: The Yellowstone River is the longest what in the lower 48 states?
items.f: The river flows about 671 miles from the Absaroka Mountains to the Missouri River near the North Dakota line.

items.q: Which is the world's tallest active geyser?
items.f: Steamboat's major eruptions shoot water more than 300 feet high. It's in the Norris Geyser Basin.

items.q: Yellowstone is larger than which two states combined?
items.f: The park covers 3,472 square miles, or about 2.2 million acres.

items.q: The NPS says the travertine terraces at Mammoth Hot Springs look like what?
items.f: Hot water rising through limestone builds the terraces, and they can change shape surprisingly fast.

items.q: How many Native American tribes have historic ties to Yellowstone?
items.f: Yellowstone also has more than 1,800 known archeological sites.

items.q: About how much of Yellowstone is covered by forest?
items.f: More than 80% of that forest is lodgepole pine.

items.q: Roughly how often does Old Faithful erupt these days?
items.f: As of January 2025, the median wait between eruptions was 102 minutes (give or take 10). Intervals ranged from 54 to 118 minutes.

items.q: About how many visits did Yellowstone get in 2024?
items.f: The 2024 total was 44% higher than in 2022, when historic floods cut off access to parts of the park.

items.q: In 1901, about how many bison were counted in Yellowstone?
items.f: Congress then paid to buy 21 bison from private owners, and they were raised in the Lamar Valley to rebuild the herd.
items.s: National Park Service: Lamar Buffalo Ranch

items.q: Which is the oldest hotel still operating in Yellowstone?
items.f: It opened in 1891. Robert Reamer later added its signature columns and false balconies.
items.s: National Park Service: Lake Hotel and Cabins

items.q: Roughly when did the eruption that formed today's Yellowstone Caldera happen?
items.f: The Lava Creek eruption threw out more than 1,000 cubic kilometers of material and left a caldera about 30 by 45 miles.

items.q: Which president signed the law creating Yellowstone National Park?
items.f: Grant signed the act on March 1, 1872, only six months after the Hayden Expedition explored the area.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: The terraces at Mammoth Hot Springs are made of what?
items.f: The travertine terraces are always changing, sometimes within a single day.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: Which area has the most geysers in Yellowstone?
items.f: At least 150 hydrothermal features are packed into about one square mile around Old Faithful.

items.q: How fast can a bison run?
items.f: Bison can also jump over objects about 5 feet high. Bulls weigh up to about 2,000 pounds.

items.q: In 1959, a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck just west of Yellowstone near which lake?
items.f: By the next day, at least 289 springs in the Firehole River basins had erupted as geysers, and 160 of them had no record of ever erupting before.

items.q: People have been quarrying Yellowstone's Obsidian Cliff for toolmaking for more than how long?
items.f: Obsidian Cliff became a National Historic Landmark in 1996.

items.q: What words are carved on the Roosevelt Arch at the North Entrance?
items.a: For the benefit and enjoyment of the people
items.f: President Theodore Roosevelt placed the arch's cornerstone in 1903, and you can still drive through it all year.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: What gives the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone its yellow walls?
items.a: Iron in rock altered by hot water
items.f: Hot water altered the rhyolite rock, and the iron in it oxidized. The NPS says most of the yellows come from iron and sulfur in the rock.
items.s: National Park Service: Canyon Village and the Grand Canyon

items.q: West Thumb's Fishing Cone got its name because early visitors did what there?
w: Caught fish in its hot water
Used it as a fish hatchery
Spotted fossils of fish in it
items.f: People caught trout in the lake and cooked them in the boiling spring while they were still on the hook. It's banned now because it damaged the cone.

items.q: How close can you legally get to bears and wolves in Yellowstone?
items.f: Stay at least 25 yards from all other animals, including bison and elk.

items.q: Why has Morning Glory Pool lost much of its deep blue color?
items.a: Visitors threw coins and trash in
items.f: The junk clogged the vent and the water cooled, so orange and yellow bacteria spread toward the center of the pool.
items.s: National Park Service: Morning Glory Pool

items.q: Which gateway town sits at Yellowstone's North Entrance?
items.f: The North Entrance is marked by the Roosevelt Arch, and Gardiner is also home to the park's Heritage and Research Center.
items.s: National Park Service: Mammoth Hot Springs and the North

items.q: In what year were gray wolves brought back to Yellowstone?
items.f: The park's last wolf pack was killed in 1926. In 1995 and 1996, 31 gray wolves from western Canada were moved to Yellowstone.
items.s: National Park Service: History of Wolf Management

items.q: About how many hydrothermal features does Yellowstone have?
items.f: That count includes more than 500 active geysers, which is over half of all the geysers in the world.

items.q: Who was Yellowstone's first superintendent?
items.f: Langford took the job even though it came with no pay.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: French traders gave the Yellowstone River what name?
items.f: The Hidatsa named the river for the yellow sandstone bluffs along it in eastern Montana. French traders translated that name as 'Roche Jaune,' which means 'yellow rock.'

items.q: Whose photographs, along with Thomas Moran's paintings, helped convince Congress to protect Yellowstone?
items.f: Jackson's photographs and Moran's paintings showed lawmakers back East what the West really looked like.
items.s: National Park Service: Birth of a National Park

items.q: In 1877, which people crossed Yellowstone in 13 days while fleeing the U.S. Army?
items.f: About 800 men, women and children, with almost 2,000 horses, entered the park on August 23, 1877.
items.s: National Park Service: Flight of the Nez Perce

items.q: How many entrances does Yellowstone have?
items.f: The park has 392 miles of paved roads and more than 15 miles of boardwalk.

items.q: Obsidian from Yellowstone's Obsidian Cliff has been found as far away as which region?
items.f: It's the source of about 90% of the obsidian found at Hopewell mound sites in the Ohio River Valley.

items.q: Which non-native fish threatens native cutthroat trout in Yellowstone Lake?
items.f: Gillnetting is the park's main tool for reducing the lake trout population. Crews set the nets in deep water to avoid catching cutthroat.

items.q: What is the largest hot spring in Yellowstone?
items.f: Grand Prismatic is 200 to 330 feet across and more than 121 feet deep. Its rainbow rings come from heat-loving microbes called thermophiles.
items.s: National Park Service: Grand Prismatic Spring

items.q: Which Yellowstone entrance is open to regular cars all year?
items.f: The only road usually open to regular vehicles all year runs from the North Entrance at Gardiner, Montana, through Tower Junction to Cooke City.

items.q: Which is Yellowstone's hottest thermal area?
items.f: A scientific drill hole at Norris recorded 459°F just 1,087 feet below the surface, the highest temperature measured in any Yellowstone thermal area.
items.s: National Park Service: Norris Geyser Basin

items.q: Why is fishing banned at Fishing Bridge?
items.f: Overfishing had helped cause the trout's decline, so the bridge closed to fishing in 1973. Now it's a good place to watch trout instead.
